L174: Row Level Security
L175: 
L176: Secure your data using Postgres Row Level Security.
L177: 
L178: Postgres cite131†Row Level Security (RLS)†www.postgresql.org gives you granular authorization rules that run inside the database.
L179: 
L180: A table in an exposed schema without RLS is readable and writable by any role with a grant on it. Enable RLS on every table in an exposed schema. On projects that still grant `anon` and `authenticated` by default, revoke those grants. Adding policies doesn't remove them.
L181: 
L182: Use the guide in three parts:
L183:   * cite132†Understand Row Level Security explains how grants and policies combine to control access.
L184:   * cite133†Secure a table with RLS is the procedure to follow for every table in an exposed schema: grants, policies, and `supabase test db`.
L185:   * cite134†RLS reference documents the helper functions and patterns you use inside a policy expression.
L186: 
L187: Read the first section when you're deciding how to model access. Go directly to the second section when you're ready to secure a table.
L188: ## Understand Row Level Securitycite132†# L189: ### What a policy doescite135†# L190: 
L191: cite136†Policies†www.postgresql.org are Postgres's rule engine. Each policy is attached to a table, and the policy is executed every time a table is accessed.
L192: 
L193: Think of a policy as adding a `WHERE` clause to every query. A policy like this:
L194: 
L195:     `
L196: 
L197:     1
L198: 
L199:     create policy "Individuals can view their own todos."
L200: 
L201:     2
L202: 
L203:     on todos for select
L204: 
L205:     3
L206: 
L207:     to authenticated
L208: 
L209:     4
L210: 
L211:     using ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id );
L212: 
L213:     `
L214: That policy translates to this whenever a user selects from the todos table:
L215: 
L216:     `
L217: 
L218:     1
L219: 
L220:     select *
L221: 
L222:     2
L223: 
L224:     from todos
L225: 
L226:     3
L227: 
L228:     where auth.uid() = todos.user_id;
L229: 
L230:     4
L231: 
L232:     -- Policy is implicitly added.
L233: 
L234:     `
L235: You write RLS rules in SQL, so a rule can express whatever access logic your app needs. Because RLS is a Postgres primitive, it also protects your data when it is reached through third-party tooling, which is what makes it "cite137†defense in depth†en.wikipedia.org ". Combine RLS with cite138†Supabase Auth for end-to-end user security from the browser to the database.
L236: ### Grants and policiescite139†# L237: 
L238: Postgres runs two checks before a client touches a table. Grants decide whether a role can run an operation on the table at all. Policies decide which rows that operation applies to. Set both for every table you expose.
L239: 
L240: On existing projects, a new table in `public` starts with every privilege already granted to all three roles:
L241: Role  | Granted automatically  | What it should keep
L242: --- | --- | ---
L243: `anon`  | `select`, `insert`, `update`, `delete`  | Only what signed-out visitors are meant to read
L244: `authenticated`  | `select`, `insert`, `update`, `delete`  | Only the operations your app exposes to signed-in users
L245: `service_role`  | `select`, `insert`, `update`, `delete`  | Full access. It bypasses RLS, so keep it server-side
L246: Adding policies doesn't take those grants back. A table protected only by policies still hands `anon` an insert path if you never revoke the grant.
L247: 
L248: Not every project grants these automatically. See cite140†Default privileges . Grant each role only the operations it needs.
L249: 
L250: A missing grant raises a `42501` error before any policy runs. When a request fails that your policy should allow, check the grants before you change the policy. To set them, see cite141†Enable RLS and set the grants .
L251: ### Authenticated and unauthenticated rolescite142†# L252: 
L253: Supabase maps every request to one of the roles:
L254: 
L255:   * `anon`: an unauthenticated request (the user is not signed in)
L256:   * `authenticated`: an authenticated request (the user is signed in)
L257: These are cite31†Postgres Roles . You can use these roles within your Policies using the `TO` clause:
L258: 
L259:     `
L260: 
L261:     1
L262: 
L263:     create policy "Profiles are viewable by everyone"
L264: 
L265:     2
L266: 
L267:     on profiles for select
L268: 
L269:     3
L270: 
L271:     to authenticated, anon
L272: 
L273:     4
L274: 
L275:     using ( true );
L276: 
L277:     5
L278: 
L279:     6
L280: 
L281:     -- OR
L282: 
L283:     7
L284: 
L285:     8
L286: 
L287:     create policy "Public profiles are viewable only by authenticated users"
L288: 
L289:     9
L290: 
L291:     on profiles for select
L292: 
L293:     10
L294:     to authenticated
L295: 
L296:     11
L297: 
L298:     using ( true );
L299: 
L300:     `
L301: Anonymous user vs the anon key
L302: 
L303: Using the `anon` Postgres role is different from an cite143†anonymous user in Supabase Auth. An anonymous user assumes the `authenticated` role to access the database and can be differentiated from a permanent user by checking the `is_anonymous` claim in the JWT.
L304: 
L305: A policy that reads `to anon using ( true )` grants every unauthenticated visitor read access to every row the role can already reach through grants. Use it only for data that is meant to be public.
L306: ### Views and RLScite144†# L307: 
L308: Views bypass RLS by default because they are usually created with the `postgres` user. This is a feature of Postgres, which automatically creates views with `security definer`. A view over a protected table hands out every row its policies were meant to withhold, so a view needs the same attention as a table. To create one safely, see cite145†Expose a view safely .
L309: ## Secure a table with RLScite133†# L310: 
L311: Follow these steps for every table in an exposed schema:
L312: 
L313:   1. cite141†Enable RLS and set the grants to match the app.
L314:   2. cite146†Write a policy per operation .
L315:   3. cite147†Create a `.sql` file under `supabase/tests/` that asserts allow and deny for `select`, `insert`, `update`, and `delete`, for `anon` and `authenticated`.
L316:   4. cite148†Run `supabase test db` and fix what it reports.
L317: 
L318: Until the suite passes, you don't know whether the policies do what you intended.
L319: ### Enable RLS and set the grantscite141†# L320: 
L321: Run these statements in the cite149†SQL Editor for a one-off change, or in a cite150†migration to keep the change reproducible across environments. Grants and RLS belong in the same migration.
L322: 
L323: Enable RLS, then set the grants to match what each role does in your app:
L324: 
L325:   1. Enable RLS on the table.
L326: 
L327:     `
L328: 
L329:     1
L330: 
L331:     alter table public.reports enable row level security;
L332: 
L333:     `
L334: Once RLS is enabled, no data is accessible through the cite151†API when using a publishable key, until you create policies.
L335: 
L336:   2. Revoke any existing grants from both client roles.
L337: 
L338:     `
L339: 
L340:     1
L341: 
L342:     revoke all on table public.reports from anon, authenticated;
L343: 
L344:     `
